— After 157 days, Mr. Araghchi says, “The Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding is no longer on the table and has no practical relevance.” This is called eating your own words (licking your own spit). The Islamabad agreement was fraudulent in its own ways because it came at the cost of selling Iran’s dignity and the norms established by the martyred Leader. It was so vague and erroneous that the Leader himself held a different view of it. In a recent exposition, it was reported that the Leader (Imam Mujtaba Khamenei) called the Islamabad negotiation team “incompetent and unaware of the outcomes.” This raises serious questions about Mr. Marandi and many apologists like him, who twist facts for anything, like trimming rocks, to justify the actions of the Foreign Ministry simply because it is their profession and nothing else. Those who exposed its flaws and criticised its vagueness were right. Neither Nabavian nor Foad Izadi, nor the others, were wrong. It was Mr. Qalibaf who halted the functioning of parliament to suppress and silence the opposition. Today, after 157 days, Araghchi, the main figure behind it, is eating his own words. If this continues, new abasement and shame will return to their faces. The fundamental problem was never merely the wording of the memorandum, but the political approach that produced it, the concessions it entailed, which were compromising, tantamount to surrender, and extremely weak in their approach, and the attempt to present it as a diplomatic achievement despite the serious questions surrounding its terms and implications. When criticism was raised, instead of addressing those concerns with transparency and accountability, many chose to dismiss the critics, defend the negotiating team, and portray scepticism as opposition to diplomacy itself. Diplomacy, however, cannot be treated as an unquestionable virtue regardless of its substance or consequences. A negotiation must be judged by what it secures, what it compromises, and whether it preserves the dignity, strategic interests, and principles of the nation. Now the question arises: What has actually been achieved? Now that the very figure who championed this process has declared the memorandum irrelevant, those who spent months defending it should also confront the contradictions in their own arguments. They cannot indefinitely demand that others forget their earlier statements while expecting their own justifications to remain beyond scrutiny. Political accountability requires consistency, honesty, and the willingness to acknowledge mistakes, particularly when the decisions in question concern the blood, sacrifices, and national interests of a country that has endured immense hardship and continues to endure it. The issue is not whether negotiations should take place. Nepal PM Balendra Shah Begins Two-Day Visit to India Nepal Prime Minister Balendra Shah departed for New Delhi on November 22 for a two-day official visit at the invitation of his Indian counterpart, Narendra Modi. It is Shah’s first bilateral trip abroad since he took office in March. Shah is scheduled to meet Indian External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar on Sunday. On November 23, he will hold talks with Modi and meet President Droupadi Murmu. The two prime ministers are expected to exchange documents and make a joint statement after their talks. The discussions are expected to cover trade and investment, energy and water resources, transport and digital connectivity, technology and innovation. Nepal’s Foreign Ministry has also said the sides are expected to sign agreements in areas including education, healthcare, agriculture, sports and disaster management. Reconstruction following devastating floods in Nepal in August and improved air connectivity may also feature in the talks. Kathmandu has sought additional air-entry routes through India to improve access to Bhairahawa and Pokhara. India is Nepal’s largest trading partner and a major bilateral aid donor. The outcomes of the visit are expected after Shah’s meeting with Modi on Monday.
